instruction: Design the main gameplay screen (a single page) for a Crossy Road-style road-crossing game. Include a charming animal player, several horizontal terrain lanes, moving cars or trucks, a river or grass safety strip, score and best-score HUD, and compact four-direction controls. Use perspective and scale to make the crossing route immediately legible. Put strong emphasis on playful low-poly character, clear hazards, depth, color rhythm, and a polished game-ready composition.

history.critique: Brief & Intent: The 'charming animal player' is a ~10px frog stranded at the TOP of the board — the brief's central emphasis (playful low-poly character) is effectively absent, and its top placement contradicts the bottom-to-top crossing convention, making the route direction ambiguous. The bottom ~40% of the viewport is empty flat green, so 'several horizontal terrain lanes' and 'color rhythm' collapse into a dead zone. The two dark trucks on the second road are near-invisible against gray asphalt, failing 'clear hazards.' The right-hand control column is a tall white slab with the D-pad floating in dead space — the opposite of 'compact.' Clarity & Hierarchy: Focal priority is inverted — the loudest elements are the HUD and red Start button while the player is the quietest. The unexplained green dot in the D-pad center and the orphaned 'HOP' label add noise. Lane order (grass/river/grass/road/river/road/grass/road/void) has no consistent cadence, and with no grid, shadows, or scale cues, depth and 'which lane am I in' are unreadable. Visual System & Craft: Two mismatched card treatments (dark-bordered game panel vs. white control panel) read as separate widgets, not one device. Vehicles lack a shared design kit: red/blue cars have cabins and wheels, the orange bus is a flat slab, the trucks are blobs — no headlights/taillights, no ground shadows, so nothing feels grounded. The river is a flat blue band with static squiggles; grass is a flat fill with random 'W' glyphs and tiny flower crosses that form no tile system. Background blobs (dot-circle, squiggle, rounded rect) are generic decoration unrelated to the game's identity. Expressiveness & Distinctiveness: No perspective or scale, no character personality, no lane-specific props (logs, lily pads, trees), no motion cues — the scene reads as a flat UI mock, not a game-ready composition; the 'Hoppy Hop' pun and frog chip are the only authored moments. Real trade-offs: (1) True perspective vs. offline flat craft — full 3D is out of scope, but a subtle vertical scale gradient + shadows fakes depth cheaply. (2) A large readable player vs. lane density — the player must own the bottom starting lane, converting the empty green from dead space into functional content. (3) Hazard contrast vs. palette harmony — vehicles need outlines/lights that pop against gray without introducing new hues. (4) Compact side controls vs. game-native overlay — a side panel is acceptable on desktop but must shrink to hug the pad; overlaying on the viewport is more game-like at the cost of some play area.
history.suggestion: Prioritized plan: 1) Player first — build a layered low-poly frog (body, big eyes, folded legs) at ~56–64px with an elliptical contact shadow and a 2-frame idle bob, placed centered on a new bottom starting grass lane so the crossing reads bottom→top; this single fix resolves the brief's core emphasis and the inverted focal hierarchy. 2) Fill the void — replace the empty green with the starting lane (tile grid, 2–3 low-poly trees, flowers) and rebalance the stack to a strict grass/road/river cadence that fills the viewport edge-to-edge, restoring color rhythm. 3) Fake depth — scale lanes and vehicles ~10% larger toward the bottom, add per-vehicle drop shadows and a slightly darker top edge per lane; keeps everything flat and offline while making the route legible. 4) Vehicle kit — one shared SVG/CSS template (rounded body, cabin, wheels, white headlight dots on the leading edge, red taillights, 2px dark outline, ground shadow); recolor the two dark trucks to mid-gray or add strong outlines so every hazard reads at a glance. 5) Compact controls — shrink the right panel to hug the D-pad (or overlay the pad bottom-right of the viewport), remove or icon-label the center dot, and move Start into the HUD or as a 'Tap to hop' overlay on the board. 6) Identity & motion pass — unify border-radius/shadow tokens across both panels, swap background blobs for faint frog/leaf motifs in the lane palette, and add CSS keyframe motion (river drift, flower sway, scrolling cars) so the draft feels game-ready.

1. Player character: draw a proper low-poly-style frog (layered SVG/CSS shapes: body, eyes, legs) at ~56px, place it at the bottom-center starting lane, add a soft elliptical shadow and a subtle idle bob. This is the single biggest fix for brief alignment and focal hierarchy.
2. Rebuild the lane stack to fill the viewport: starting grass lane (with tile grid + a few trees/flowers), then road, river, grass, road, river, road, grass, road — no empty zone; keep the 3–4 lane rhythm.
